fetched_contents.text: pH-Responsive Hydrogels: Recent Advances in Pharmaceutical Applications Abstract Hydrogels are three-dimensional polymeric systems, being able to accommodate different categories of bioactive agents and act as promising drug delivery systems in many different biomedical applications. Due to their extended 3D network, hydrogels exhibit many advantages, such as extensive loading capacity and controlled drug release profiles, combined with characteristics such as biocompatibility and biodegradability, due to their constructive polymeric biomaterials. Moreover, hydrogels are capable of being administered via different routes of administration, including systemic and topical ones, due to their tunable characteristics. Stimuli-responsive hydrogels are characterized as smart biomaterials, while environmental stimuli, such as pH, can be employed to trigger on-demand drug release from the hydrogels via the provocation of conformational changes. In the present study, an emphasis on the pH-responsive hydrogels is taking place through various literature cases in drug delivery, wound healing, and some alternative applications, including implantation, oral administration, etc., wherein many different polymeric derivatives have been utilized. Moreover, the role of each used polymer or polymeric combination with other functional biomaterials, their mode of structure formation (for example, crosslinking), and their content release mechanism are highlighted, as well as the therapeutic effect of the hydrogels on different pathological conditions, as promising candidates for pharmaceutical applications. Keywords: pH-responsive, hydrogels, drug delivery, polymers, wound healing, chitosan, poly(acrylic acid), controlled release, anticancer therapy 1. Introduction Hydrogels are three-dimensional polymeric systems formed through chemical bonds (covalent bonds) and physical interactions (e.g., hydrogen bonds, Coulombic forces, Van der Waals, coordination bonds, etc.) [1,2,3,4]. Drug molecules, bioactive chemicals, natural goods, nutritional additives, and biomolecules are just a few of the many content categories that can be loaded into hydrogels. In addition to their tunable solubility, high water absorption capacity, and moisture retention [3], hydrogels’ extended 3D interior surface gives them a high loading/encapsulation efficiency, making them perfect for drug delivery applications. They also have the potential to hold large amounts of water molecules through capillary action and osmotic pressure, making them resemble the extracellular matrices of living tissues [4]. Their main advantages include a profile of high safety with low immunogenicity, high biocompatibility, biodegradability, and cytocompatibility due to the sustainability of their used constructive polymeric biomaterials, along with some structural characteristics such as mechanical stability, high loading capacity, controlled release ability, adhesive properties, and tunable chemical structure that can be modified towards enhancing targeting ability and triggered content release (Scheme 1) [5]. However, some of their drawbacks include some scale-up limitations, such as batch-to-batch variability and fragile mechanical strengths, along with some biodegradation phenomena that should be under continuous control, such as catabolization, gelation, and microbial instability [6,7]. Stimuli-responsive hydrogels can be considered as smart biomaterials, while the external triggers and environmental variations, such as pH, temperature, electrical and magnetic fields, light, and biomolecule concentration such as elevated ROS levels, high glucose concentrations, and overexpressed enzymes, can be employed to trigger on-demand drug release from the hydrogels. From a biological point of view, variations in pH are known to take place at several body sites, such as the gastrointestinal tract, vagina, and blood vessels, which can provide a suitable condition for pH-responsive drug release, as well as within intracellular compartments, such as endosomal/lysosomal, and also in cases of pathological conditions, such as oxidative stress and tumor microenvironment. pH-responsive hydrogels are capable of being designed and customized to exhibit a site-specific response to particular pH ranges, enabling controlled drug release in these specific pH environments via pH-dependent swelling or collapse behavior [7]. pH-responsive hydrogels are composed of polymeric backbones with ionizable functional groups [8,9]. These ionizable groups can achieve a targeted and regulated drug release in response to local pH alterations by exhibiting conformational or solubility changes or hydrogel transitioning between swelling and deswelling states. Some applications of the pH-responsive hydrogels already mentioned are gastroretentive drug delivery, intestine and colon targeting drug delivery, their utilization in protein or peptide delivery, in transdermal patches, and for cancer targeting, with the aim of enhancing treatment effectiveness and preventing side effects [8,9]. In the present study, emphasis is given to the application of the pH-responsive hydrogels, providing a variety of literature studies in drug delivery, wound healing, and some alternative applications, including implantation, oral administration, etc., by examining cases comprising many different polymeric candidates [7]. Namely, a detailed description of different pH-responsive hydrogels is presented, highlighting the role of each polymer utilized or of the combination of different polymers or the combination with other functional biomaterials, their mode of structure formation (for example, crosslinking), their content release mechanism, as well as their therapeutic effect on different pathological conditions, as promising candidates for biomedical applications (Figure 1). 2. Submission received: 11 October 2024 / Revised: 6 November 2024 / Accepted: 9 November 2024 / Published: 12 November 2024 Abstract Hyaluronic acid, a biocompatible polymer, holds significant potential for drug delivery applications. Its variable degree of protonation, which entails tunable physical properties, makes it an ideal candidate for developing pH-sensitive hydrogels. Like other smart drug delivery systems, pH-responsive hydrogels can enhance medical treatment and expedite the healing process. However, the inherent complexity of hydrogels poses challenges in identifying suitable matrix systems. This study evaluates the potential of thiolated hyaluronic acid hydrogels, physically cross-linked with deacetylated disaccharide units of the polymer, for use in drug delivery. Using low-molecular-weight dextrans as model drugs, we investigated the system’s response to different pH environments in terms of swelling as well as the kinetic and mechanistic release of the encapsulated compound. The data suggest tunable release properties of the gel regarding drug size and pH value. Our results demonstrate the gel system’s potential for smart drug delivery. We anticipate that this system is a promising candidate for use in transdermal wound healing applications and strongly encourage further investigations using other sorts of (model) drugs to gain a more detailed insight into its pH-responsive transport qualities. Graphical Abstract 1. Introduction Throughout the past few years, the design of adaptable drug delivery systems has increasingly become a goal of the development of novel materials. In particular, the release of active compounds as a response to environmental changes such as the pH represents a commonly approached strategy for the highly effective treatment of wounds [1]. Being an endogenous non-sulfated saccharide polymer, hyaluronic acid (HA) is known to function as a biocompatible material. Due to its polyanionic, linear structure consisting of repetitive disaccharide units, HA is able to efficiently bind water and several kinds of protein structures [2], which renders the polymer a crucial structural component of the extracellular matrix (ECM) contributing to wound healing processes [2,3]. In general, pH-dependent swelling of hydrogels relies on the pH of the surrounding medium relative to the acidic or basic moiety’s pKa or pKb [4] As for HA, the deprotonation of carboxylic acid moieties occurs within a medium of pH > pKa = 3, generating fixed negative charges on the polymer chains and mobile positive charges in the solution [5]. This leads to an increase in hydrophilicity, the number of immobilized negative charges, and electrostatic repulsion between the chains [5,6], resulting in a higher uptake of water and thus swelling of the hydrogel [7]. Since drug delivery systems can differ in many ways, such as their molecular structure or behavior toward different kinds of stimuli [8], it is essential to keep in mind that varying the matrix material and environmental conditions will lead to different release kinetics. Finding a way to model the release of a drug in order to compare different parameters is therefore crucial to identify the most suitable one for the application of the desired drug. While, in general, there are no restrictions when it comes to finding the best fitting function to a set of data, some models have proven to suit drug release data more often than others (Table 1). A broadly used semi-empirical model was established by Higuchi [9]. As a special case of the Korsmeyer–Peppas model [10,11,12], it depicts the ratio of target concentration ct to the maximum target concentration c∞ in the surrounding medium after when approaching infinity as a function of the square root of the time t. The rate constant k varies from model to model. The exponent n allows conclusions regarding the type of release kinetics and is dependent on the hydrogel’s geometry (Table 2). A solely diffusion-caused release is described by Fick’s law, whereas the zero-order model, also termed Case II transport, describes linear non-Fickian kinetics, stating that the release is controlled by relaxation or swelling of the matrix. Values in between these extremes are considered hybrid release mechanisms and are called anomalous [12,14]. Values of n that are lower than the tabular Fickian diffusion value still indicate a diffusion-controlled mechanism [15,16]; however, they can indicate a hampered variation of transport [17]. Other models, like Peppas–Sahlin’s [13], are able to estimate the proportion of Fickian and Case II contributions by superposition of the two. Lastly, there are several non-empirical equations, such as first-order [10,18] and second-order [18], as well as logarithmic models that can correspond to the raised data. In some cases, finding an appropriate model for drug delivery devices can be particularly challenging. These circumstances can often be traced back to a phenomenon called initial burst [19]. fetched_contents.text: pH Sensitive Hydrogels in Drug Delivery: Brief History, Properties, Swelling, and Release Mechanism, Material Selection and Applications Abstract Improving the safety efficacy ratio of existing drugs is a current challenge to be addressed rather than the development of novel drugs which involve much expense and time. The efficacy of drugs is affected by a number of factors such as their low aqueous solubility, unequal absorption along the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, risk of degradation in the acidic milieu of the stomach, low permeation of the drugs in the upper GI tract, systematic side effects, etc. This review aims to enlighten readers on the role of pH sensitive hydrogels in drug delivery, their mechanism of action, swelling, and drug release as a function of pH change along the GI tract. The basis for the selection of materials, their structural features, physical and chemical properties, the presence of ionic pendant groups, and the influence of their pKa and pKb values on the ionization, consequent swelling, and targeted drug release are also highlighted. Keywords: pH sensitive hydrogels, swelling and drug release mechanism, biocompatible materials, drug delivery applications 1. Introduction 1.1. Brief History of Hydrogels The term hydrogel dates back to 1894 when this term was used by Lee et al. [1] for colloidal gels of certain inorganic salts. These gels are quite the opposite of the materials which are described by the term hydrogel today [2]. The first ever hydrogel reported in 1949 for biomedical implant was poly(vinyl alcohol) cross-linked with formaldehyde and marketed with the trade name Ivalon [3]. Later in 1958, Danno prepared poly(vinyl alcohol) hydrogels cross-linked by passing gamma irradiation through an aqueous solution [4]. The synthesis of poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) (pHEMA) gels for contact lens application by Wichterle and Lim [5] in 1960 was the revolution for present day hydrogels. pHEMA exhibited the characteristic properties of modern hydrogels like cross-linked networks that can show swelling upon absorption of excess of water without dissolution and can also retain their shape [6]. The synthesis of pHEMA was also previously reported by du Pont de Nemours scientists in their publication in 1936 describing it as a hard, brittle and glassy polymer [7]. The development of hydrogels for biomedical applications gained particular attention in the 1970s especially in the field of stimuli sensitive hydrogels, the so called smart hydrogels of modern times. The first pH sensitive hydrogel was synthesized in 1971 by Kopecek. The author introduced inorganic groups on the pHEMA backbone to manipulate the pH sensitivity in the pHEMA membranes and studied NaCl permeability control of these membranes as a function of pH [8]. Hydrogel structure and release mechanisms are strongly pH-dependent because pH changes alter ionizable group ionization, crosslinking interactions, and the overall conformational state of the polymeric network. The evidence shows that pH-responsive hydrogels are composed of polymeric backbones with ionizable functional groups, and these groups can change conformation or solubility in response to local pH, triggering swelling, collapse, or structural transitions [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]. This is central to the mechanism of pH-sensitive release.

On whether pH causes swelling, dissociation, or structural changes: the evidence indicates that pH can induce swelling, collapse, or conformational shifts in the hydrogel. One review states that pH-responsive hydrogels can exhibit conformational changes or hydrogel transitioning between swelling and deswelling states in response to pH changes [N1-F1]. Another source notes that pH-dependent swelling is tied to the pH of the surrounding medium relative to the acidic or basic moiety’s pKa or pKb [N2-F2]. In the case of hyaluronic acid hydrogels, the deprotonation of carboxylic acid moieties at pH > pKa = 3 generates fixed negative charges on the polymer chains, increases hydrophilicity, and electrostatic repulsion, leading to higher water uptake and swelling [N2-F2]. This means that pH changes can cause dissociation-like effects through ionization of functional groups, structural expansion through swelling, or structural contraction through collapse, depending on the hydrogel chemistry and the direction of pH shift [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-F2].

On how ionizable groups or crosslinking chemistry respond to pH changes: ionizable groups are the primary pH sensors in these systems. The review explains that pH-sensitive hydrogels contain polymeric backbones with ionizable functional groups, and these groups can achieve targeted and regulated drug release by exhibiting conformational or solubility changes [N1-R2][N1-F1]. For example, the pKa of poly(acrylic acid) is around 4.5–5.0, and at pH > 5, acidic moieties become ionized, developing a negative charge on the polymer chains [N3-R1]. Similarly, hyaluronic acid hydrogels show pH-dependent swelling because HA’s deprotonation at pH > pKa = 3 generates fixed negative charges and electrostatic repulsion, increasing swelling [N2-F2]. Crosslinking chemistry also matters: hydrogels can be chemically crosslinked by covalent bonds or physically crosslinked by secondary interactions such as hydrogen bonding, and these crosslinking modes influence how the hydrogel responds to pH. Chemical crosslinking provides structural stability, while physical crosslinking may allow more reversible or sensitive pH responses [N3-F3]. The evidence also highlights that hydrogel dissolution can occur in some pH media, which changes the apparent structural behavior [N6-R3]. Therefore, pH effects are not only about ionizable groups but also about how the crosslinked network is held together and whether that network can dissolve or swell in response to the environment.

On which release mechanisms are most sensitive to pH variation: the evidence suggests that swelling-driven and diffusion-driven release are most sensitive to pH variation. In the hyaluronic acid hydrogel study, pH-dependent swelling was directly linked to drug release, and the authors note that release can be diffusion-controlled, Case II transport-controlled, or a hybrid of both, depending on hydrogel geometry and environmental conditions [N2-F2]. The review on pH-responsive hydrogels also states that pH shifts can alter the interaction of hydrogel polymer chains, triggering drug release from pH-sensitive hydrogels [N1-R4]. In practical terms, pH-sensitive swelling is the most direct mechanism: when pH causes the hydrogel to expand, it increases the surface area and porosity available for drug diffusion, while pH-induced collapse reduces porosity and slows release [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Ionizable groups and crosslinking chemistry therefore determine which release mechanism dominates. The review further notes that varying the matrix material and environmental conditions leads to different release kinetics, so pH can act as a tuning parameter rather than a fixed trigger [N2-F2]. In short, the mechanisms most sensitive to pH are swelling, ionization-induced conformational changes, and any diffusion or transport mechanism that depends on the hydrogel’s physical state [N1-F1][N2-F2][N1-R4].

Release profiling methods shape how pH effects are interpreted because each method measures different aspects of drug release and may emphasize some effects while obscuring others. The evidence shows that common methods include dialysis, sample-and-separate, and USP apparatus, while newer approaches such as numerical deconvolution can provide more detailed kinetic insight [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4]. These methods are used to monitor batch-to-batch quality and understand drug release in in vitro conditions [N4-R3]. However, the same evidence also indicates that interpretation depends on what exactly is measured and how the system is set up.

What each release method measures and how it captures pH effects: dialysis is a widely used and versatile method for testing in vitro drug release of particulate formulations [N4-R4]. It measures the amount of drug diffusing across a semi-permeable membrane into a receiving medium, which can reflect both diffusion and some swelling-driven release. The USP apparatus, particularly USP Apparatus 3, is also used in pH studies, and the evidence notes that release can vary with the apparatus used and stirring conditions [N4-R5]. Sample-and-separate and other methods are described as part of the broader current in vitro dissolution/release testing strategy [N4-R1]. Numerical deconvolution is a newer method that can evaluate actual drug release kinetics inside the donor, suggesting that it may capture more mechanistic details than simple cumulative release measurements [N4-R2]. For pH studies, this matters because swelling, ionization, and collapse can affect the hydrogel’s porosity and the effective diffusion path, which may not be fully captured by a single cumulative release measurement [N2-F2][N1-R4].

Limitations of dialysis, USP apparatus, and other methods for pH studies: dialysis is versatile but may not fully mimic in vivo transport because it relies on a semi-permeable membrane and fixed pH conditions in the receiving medium [N4-R4]. The USP apparatus is useful for standardization, but the evidence shows that release can differ between apparatus types and stirring rates [N4-R5]. This means that observed release profiles may reflect method-specific behavior rather than the true pH-dependent response. The evidence also implies that release kinetics can be influenced by the geometry of the system, the model drug, and the model matrix, so a method that emphasizes one parameter may miss others [N2-F2]. In addition, the evidence notes that the same drug can have different release profiles when tested in different matrices, which suggests that method choice can confound pH effects with matrix effects [N2-F2].

How experimental design affects observed release profiles: experimental design is central to interpretation. The evidence states that varying the matrix material and environmental conditions leads to different release kinetics, and finding a suitable model for drug release is therefore crucial [N2-F2]. This means that pH effects can be amplified, suppressed, or misinterpreted if the hydrogel is not properly characterized or if the pH gradient is not controlled. The review also notes that the choice of model drug and the way the system is modeled can strongly influence the observed release profile [N2-F2]. Dialysis and USP methods may not fully capture the hydrogel’s three-dimensional structure, the swelling response, or the interplay between pH and drug solubility, whereas more sophisticated deconvolution-based methods can reveal underlying kinetics [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Overall, release profiling methods influence interpretation by determining whether the observed profile reflects pH-driven swelling, diffusion, matrix relaxation, or other effects, and by affecting the sensitivity to pH variation [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4][N2-F2].

The evidence provides several examples of pH-dependent drug release profiles in hydrogel systems, showing faster, slower, or biphasic release at different pH values, as well as changes in release kinetics and cumulative release. The most direct example is a hyaluronic acid hydrogel study, which reports pH-dependent swelling and links that swelling to release behavior [N2-F2]. In another example, a study on polymeric nanogels reports pH-dependent release, with 10–12% release at pH 1.2 and 79.5–91% release at pH 6.8 [N2-R4]. This is a clear case of faster release at higher pH, showing that the hydrogel’s structure becomes more permeable or swollen under physiological conditions. The evidence also notes that the release of theophylline, a slightly soluble compound, was studied in pH-sensitive hydrogels to examine the effect of drug solubility on migration through the system [N2-R5], suggesting that release can depend both on pH and on solubility, though this is more relevant to the dissolution/solubility branch [N6-R4].

How release kinetics and cumulative release change with pH: the evidence indicates that pH can shift the kinetics from diffusion-controlled to Case II transport-controlled or hybrid behavior. The hyaluronic acid study explains that release can be described by Fickian diffusion, Case II transport, or a combination of the two, and that the exponent n in the Korsmeyer–Peppas model allows conclusions about the type of kinetics [N2-F2]. In practical terms, lower pH may slow release if it causes collapse or reduced swelling, while higher pH may accelerate release by increasing swelling and porosity [N2-F2][N1-F1]. The nanogel example also shows that cumulative release increases substantially with pH, moving from ~10% at pH 1.2 to ~90% at pH 6.8 [N2-R4]. This illustrates that pH can strongly modulate cumulative release, with the hydrogel acting as a pH-sensitive gate that opens or closes over time.

Differences between in vitro and in vivo relevance of pH effects: the evidence suggests that in vitro pH studies are useful for understanding the mechanism and tuning release, but they may not fully predict in vivo behavior. The review notes that varying the matrix material and environmental conditions leads to different release kinetics, so in vitro results must be interpreted with caution [N2-F2]. The hyaluronic acid study itself emphasizes that hydrogels are complex systems and that the same drug can exhibit different release profiles depending on the matrix and the environmental conditions [N2-F2]. The evidence also highlights that pH-responsive hydrogels are designed to respond to local pH environments in the body, such as the gastrointestinal tract, blood vessels, or intracellular compartments, which makes them promising for site-specific delivery [N1-F1]. However, the same evidence also implies that in vitro results may not fully capture the dynamic interplay between pH, hydrogel dissolution, swelling, and transport in vivo [N2-F2][N6-R3]. In other words, pH effects are often well captured in vitro, but the exact in vivo relevance depends on whether the system can maintain the intended pH response and whether other physiological factors, such as fluid flow, enzyme activity, or drug solubility, alter the observed profile [N2-F2][N6-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a clear pattern: pH can cause faster release at higher pH where swelling is favored, slower release at lower pH where collapse or reduced swelling may occur, and biphasic or nonlinear release when the system responds through a combination of diffusion, relaxation, and structural changes [N2-R4][N2-F2]. The most relevant examples are the hyaluronic acid hydrogel and the polymeric nanogel studies, which together demonstrate that pH-dependent release is not only a qualitative effect but also a quantitative one that changes kinetics and cumulative release [N2-F2][N2-R4].

Dissolution and solubility effects are important because they can modulate pH-dependent release by altering the effective diffusivity of the drug, the hydrogel’s porosity, and the apparent release mechanism. The evidence shows that drug solubility in the pH medium matters, and that solubility can be a major factor in interpreting swelling and release behavior [N2-R5][N6-R4]. The study on theophylline and metoclopramide monohydrochloride reports that the swelling and release behavior were interpreted in terms of the significant solubility of the drugs tested and their possible association [N6-R4]. This is important because a highly soluble drug may appear to release quickly even if the hydrogel itself is not swollen, while a less soluble drug may require more swelling to enable effective transport.

How hydrogel dissolution or swelling alters apparent release behavior: the evidence indicates that hydrogel dissolution can occur in some pH media, which changes the apparent release behavior. One source states that in pH 1.8 aqueous solution, the hydrogel would absorb outside water, but during this process the polymer is dissolving [N6-R3]. This means that the observed release may not reflect only diffusion or matrix relaxation; it may also reflect the hydrogel itself dissolving, which can release the drug more rapidly than a stable hydrogel would. Conversely, pH-induced swelling can increase porosity and surface area, making diffusion more favorable and release faster [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that pH-dependent swelling can alter the hydrogel’s physical state, which in turn affects release [N2-F2]. So the apparent release profile can change depending on whether the hydrogel is swelling, collapsing, or dissolving.

When pH effects are confounded by media composition or solubility: the evidence shows that confounding is common. The review on pH-sensitive hydrogels states that varying the matrix material and environmental conditions leads to different release kinetics, implying that release profiles may reflect matrix effects rather than pH alone [N2-F2]. The solubility study explicitly connects swelling and release behavior to drug solubility, suggesting that release may be dominated by solubility rather than pH under certain conditions [N6-R4]. Similarly, the evidence on hydrogel dissolution in pH 1.8 solution indicates that the surrounding medium can affect the hydrogel’s integrity and thus the observed release [N6-R3]. This matters because a hydrogel tested in a highly acidic or highly basic medium may show different behavior than the same hydrogel in physiological conditions, and because a drug that is very soluble in the test medium may appear to release faster even if the hydrogel’s pH response is weak.

In conclusion, dissolution/solubility effects modulate pH-dependent release by influencing drug mobility, hydrogel integrity, and the apparent kinetics. Solubility can make release appear faster, hydrogel dissolution can accelerate release, and media composition can confound pH effects with matrix effects [N2-R5][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Therefore, when interpreting pH-dependent release, it is essential to separate true pH sensitivity from effects caused by drug solubility and hydrogel degradation [N2-F2][N6-R4].

## Integrated explanation of how pH variation affects drug release mechanisms and profiles in hydrogel-based delivery systems

Hydrogel-based delivery systems are highly sensitive to pH variation because pH can alter the structure of the hydrogel itself, the release mechanism, and the observed release profile. Across the available evidence, pH affects drug release through three broad pathways: **structural changes in the hydrogel**, **mechanistic shifts in release behavior**, and **confounding by solubility and dissolution effects** [N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R4].

### 1) How pH affects hydrogel structure and release mechanisms

At the core of pH-sensitive hydrogels is the response of **ionizable functional groups** and **crosslinking chemistry** to changes in pH. The evidence repeatedly states that pH-responsive hydrogels are composed of polymeric backbones with ionizable functional groups, and these groups can change conformation or solubility in response to pH, triggering swelling, collapse, or structural transitions [N1-R2][N1-F1]. This means that pH variation is not a passive background condition; it actively reconfigures the hydrogel network.

#### Swelling, dissociation, or structural changes
The evidence shows that pH can cause swelling, collapse, or structural changes. One review explicitly says that pH-responsive hydrogels can exhibit conformational changes or transition between swelling and deswelling states in response to pH changes [N1-F1]. Another source notes that pH-dependent swelling is tied to the pH of the surrounding medium relative to the acidic or basic moiety’s pKa or pKb [N2-F2]. This is a textbook example of pH-induced dissociation-like behavior through ionization, followed by structural expansion.

In contrast, lower pH can cause collapse or reduced swelling. The evidence also notes that hydrogel dissolution can occur in some pH media, which changes the apparent structural behavior [N6-R3]. So pH variation can cause a spectrum of responses: swelling at higher pH, collapse at lower pH, or even partial or total hydrogel dissolution, depending on the polymer chemistry and the surrounding environment [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R3].

The evidence explains that hydrogels can be chemically crosslinked by covalent bonds or physically crosslinked by secondary interactions such as hydrogen bonding [N3-F3]. Chemical crosslinking provides structural stability, while physical crosslinking may allow more reversible or sensitive pH responses. In other words, the same pH change can produce very different structural outcomes depending on the crosslinking mode [N3-F3].

The evidence indicates that the **most sensitive mechanisms** are those tied to **swelling**, **diffusion**, and any **matrix relaxation** mechanism. In the hyaluronic acid study, pH-dependent swelling is directly linked to drug release, and the authors note that release can be diffusion-controlled, Case II transport-controlled, or a hybrid of both, depending on hydrogel geometry and environmental conditions [N2-F2]. The review on pH-responsive hydrogels also states that pH shifts can alter the interaction of hydrogel polymer chains, triggering drug release from pH-sensitive hydrogels [N1-R4].

The review emphasizes that varying the matrix material and environmental conditions leads to different release kinetics, so pH can act as a tuning parameter rather than a fixed trigger [N2-F2]. In short, the mechanisms most sensitive to pH variation are **swelling-driven release**, **ionization-induced conformational changes**, and any **diffusion or transport mechanism** that depends on the hydrogel’s physical state [N1-F1][N2-F2][N1-R4].

The evidence base supports a clear pattern: pH variation can produce **faster, slower, or biphasic release** depending on the hydrogel chemistry and the pH environment.

#### What each method measures and how it captures pH effects
Dialysis is a widely used and versatile method for testing in vitro drug release of particulate formulations [N4-R4]. It measures the amount of drug diffusing across a semi-permeable membrane into a receiving medium, which can reflect both diffusion and some swelling-driven release. The **USP apparatus**, particularly **USP Apparatus 3**, is also used in pH studies, and the evidence notes that release can vary with the apparatus used and stirring conditions [N4-R5]. **Sample-and-separate** and other methods are described as part of the broader current in vitro dissolution/release testing strategy [N4-R1]. **Numerical deconvolution** is a newer method that can evaluate actual drug release kinetics inside the donor, suggesting that it may capture more mechanistic details than simple cumulative release measurements [N4-R2].

This matters because pH-sensitive swelling, ionization-induced conformational changes, and collapse can affect the hydrogel’s porosity and the effective diffusion path, which may not be fully captured by a single cumulative release measurement [N2-F2][N1-R4].

#### Limitations of dialysis, USP apparatus, and other methods for pH studies
Dialysis is versatile but may not fully mimic in vivo transport because it relies on a semi-permeable membrane and fixed pH conditions in the receiving medium [N4-R4]. The USP apparatus is useful for standardization, but the evidence shows that release can differ between apparatus types and stirring rates [N4-R5]. This means that observed release profiles may reflect **method-specific behavior** rather than the true pH-dependent response. The evidence also implies that release kinetics can be influenced by the geometry of the system, the model drug, and the model matrix, so a method that emphasizes one parameter may miss others [N2-F2].

#### How experimental design affects observed release profiles
Experimental design is central to interpretation. The evidence states that varying the matrix material and environmental conditions leads to different release kinetics, and finding a suitable model for drug release is therefore crucial [N2-F2]. This means that pH effects can be amplified, suppressed, or misinterpreted if the hydrogel is not properly characterized or if the pH gradient is not controlled. The review also notes that the choice of model drug and the way the system is modeled can strongly influence the observed release profile [N2-F2]. Dialysis and USP methods may not fully capture the hydrogel’s three-dimensional structure, the swelling response, or the interplay between pH and drug solubility, whereas more sophisticated deconvolution-based methods can reveal underlying kinetics [N4-R2][N4-R4].

### 4) How dissolution/solubility effects modulate pH-dependent release

Dissolution and solubility effects are important because they can modulate pH-dependent release by altering the effective diffusivity of the drug, the hydrogel’s porosity, and the apparent release mechanism. The evidence shows that **drug solubility in the pH medium matters**, and that solubility can be a major factor in interpreting swelling and release behavior [N2-R5][N6-R4].

#### Whether drug solubility in the pH medium matters for release
The evidence indicates that solubility does matter. The study on theophylline and metoclopramide monohydrochloride reports that the swelling and release behavior were interpreted in terms of the significant solubility of the drugs tested and their possible association [N6-R4]. This is important because a highly soluble drug may appear to release quickly even if the hydrogel itself is not swollen, while a less soluble drug may require more swelling to enable effective transport.

#### How hydrogel dissolution or swelling alters apparent release behavior
The evidence indicates that hydrogel dissolution can occur in some pH media, which changes the apparent release behavior. One source states that in pH 1.8 aqueous solution, the hydrogel would absorb outside water, but during this process the polymer is dissolving [N6-R3]. This means that the observed release may not reflect only diffusion or matrix relaxation; it may also reflect the hydrogel itself dissolving, which can release the drug more rapidly than a stable hydrogel would. Conversely, pH-induced swelling can increase porosity and surface area, making diffusion more favorable and release faster [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that pH-dependent swelling can alter the hydrogel’s physical state, which in turn affects release [N2-F2].

#### When pH effects are confounded by media composition or solubility
The evidence shows that confounding is common. The review on pH-sensitive hydrogels states that varying the matrix material and environmental conditions leads to different release kinetics, implying that release profiles may reflect matrix effects rather than pH alone [N2-F2]. The solubility study explicitly connects swelling and release behavior to drug solubility, suggesting that release may be dominated by solubility rather than pH under certain conditions [N6-R4]. Similarly, the evidence on hydrogel dissolution in pH 1.8 solution indicates that the surrounding medium can affect the hydrogel’s integrity and thus the observed release [N6-R3]. This matters because a hydrogel tested in a highly acidic or highly basic medium may show different behavior than the same hydrogel in physiological conditions, and because a drug that is very soluble in the test medium may appear to release faster even if the hydrogel’s pH response is weak.

### 5) Bottom line: how pH variation affects the overall system

Taken together, the evidence supports a consistent picture. pH variation affects hydrogel-based delivery systems through three intertwined mechanisms:

1. **Structural changes** in the hydrogel: pH alters ionizable groups, crosslinking interactions, and the hydrogel’s conformation, causing swelling, collapse, or dissolution [N1-R2][N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R3].
2. **Mechanistic shifts** in release behavior: pH can change the kinetics from diffusion-controlled to Case II transport-controlled or hybrid behavior, and it can shift cumulative release substantially across pH values [N2-F2][N2-R4].
3. **Confounding by dissolution and solubility**: solubility can dominate release behavior, and hydrogel dissolution can accelerate apparent release, making pH effects difficult to isolate [N2-R5][N6-R4].

Because of this, pH-dependent release is not just a simple “higher pH = faster release” effect. It depends on the polymer chemistry, the hydrogel architecture, the release method, and the surrounding medium. The best-supported conclusion is that pH variation can strongly modulate drug release mechanisms and profiles in hydrogel-based delivery systems, but the observed effect must be interpreted with care, using appropriate profiling methods and accounting for solubility and dissolution effects [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R2][N6-R4].

Hydrogel structure and release mechanisms are strongly pH-dependent because pH changes alter ionizable group ionization, crosslinking interactions, and the overall conformational state of the polymeric network. The evidence shows that pH-responsive hydrogels are composed of polymeric backbones with ionizable functional groups, and these groups can change conformation or solubility in response to local pH, triggering swelling, collapse, or structural transitions [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]. This is central to the mechanism of pH-sensitive release.

On whether pH causes swelling, dissociation, or structural changes: the evidence indicates that pH can induce swelling, collapse, or conformational shifts in the hydrogel. One review states that pH-responsive hydrogels can exhibit conformational changes or hydrogel transitioning between swelling and deswelling states in response to pH changes [N1-F1]. Another source notes that pH-dependent swelling is tied to the pH of the surrounding medium relative to the acidic or basic moiety’s pKa or pKb [N2-F2]. In the case of hyaluronic acid hydrogels, the deprotonation of carboxylic acid moieties at pH > pKa = 3 generates fixed negative charges on the polymer chains, increases hydrophilicity, and electrostatic repulsion, leading to higher water uptake and swelling [N2-F2]. This means that pH changes can cause dissociation-like effects through ionization of functional groups, structural expansion through swelling, or structural contraction through collapse, depending on the hydrogel chemistry and the direction of pH shift [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-F2].

On how ionizable groups or crosslinking chemistry respond to pH changes: ionizable groups are the primary pH sensors in these systems. The review explains that pH-sensitive hydrogels contain polymeric backbones with ionizable functional groups, and these groups can achieve targeted and regulated drug release by exhibiting conformational or solubility changes [N1-R2][N1-F1]. For example, the pKa of poly(acrylic acid) is around 4.5–5.0, and at pH > 5, acidic moieties become ionized, developing a negative charge on the polymer chains [N3-R1]. Similarly, hyaluronic acid hydrogels show pH-dependent swelling because HA’s deprotonation at pH > pKa = 3 generates fixed negative charges and electrostatic repulsion, increasing swelling [N2-F2]. Crosslinking chemistry also matters: hydrogels can be chemically crosslinked by covalent bonds or physically crosslinked by secondary interactions such as hydrogen bonding, and these crosslinking modes influence how the hydrogel responds to pH. Chemical crosslinking provides structural stability, while physical crosslinking may allow more reversible or sensitive pH responses [N3-F3]. The evidence also highlights that hydrogel dissolution can occur in some pH media, which changes the apparent structural behavior [N6-R3]. Therefore, pH effects are not only about ionizable groups but also about how the crosslinked network is held together and whether that network can dissolve or swell in response to the environment.

On which release mechanisms are most sensitive to pH variation: the evidence suggests that swelling-driven and diffusion-driven release are most sensitive to pH variation. In the hyaluronic acid hydrogel study, pH-dependent swelling was directly linked to drug release, and the authors note that release can be diffusion-controlled, Case II transport-controlled, or a hybrid of both, depending on hydrogel geometry and environmental conditions [N2-F2]. The review on pH-responsive hydrogels also states that pH shifts can alter the interaction of hydrogel polymer chains, triggering drug release from pH-sensitive hydrogels [N1-R4]. In practical terms, pH-sensitive swelling is the most direct mechanism: when pH causes the hydrogel to expand, it increases the surface area and porosity available for drug diffusion, while pH-induced collapse reduces porosity and slows release [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Ionizable groups and crosslinking chemistry therefore determine which release mechanism dominates. The review further notes that varying the matrix material and environmental conditions leads to different release kinetics, so pH can act as a tuning parameter rather than a fixed trigger [N2-F2]. In short, the mechanisms most sensitive to pH are swelling, ionization-induced conformational changes, and any diffusion or transport mechanism that depends on the hydrogel’s physical state [N1-F1][N2-F2][N1-R4].

The review notes that varying the matrix material and environmental conditions leads to different release kinetics, so in vitro results must be interpreted with caution [N2-F2]. The hyaluronic acid study itself emphasizes that hydrogels are complex systems and that the same drug can exhibit different release profiles depending on the matrix and the environmental conditions [N2-F2]. ## Integrated explanation of how pH variation affects drug release mechanisms and profiles in hydrogel-based delivery systems

Hydrogel-based delivery systems are highly sensitive to pH variation because pH can alter the structure of the hydrogel itself, the release mechanism, and the observed release profile. Across the available evidence, pH affects drug release through three broad pathways: **structural changes in the hydrogel**, **mechanistic shifts in release behavior**, and **confounding by solubility and dissolution effects** [N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R4].

### 1) How pH affects hydrogel structure and release mechanisms

At the core of pH-sensitive hydrogels is the response of **ionizable functional groups** and **crosslinking chemistry** to changes in pH. The evidence repeatedly states that pH-responsive hydrogels are composed of polymeric backbones with ionizable functional groups, and these groups can change conformation or solubility in response to pH, triggering swelling, collapse, or structural transitions [N1-R2][N1-F1]. This means that pH variation is not a passive background condition; it actively reconfigures the hydrogel network.

#### Swelling, dissociation, or structural changes
The evidence shows that pH can cause swelling, collapse, or structural changes. One review explicitly says that pH-responsive hydrogels can exhibit conformational changes or transition between swelling and deswelling states in response to pH changes [N1-F1]. Another source notes that pH-dependent swelling is tied to the pH of the surrounding medium relative to the acidic or basic moiety’s pKa or pKb [N2-F2]. In the case of hyaluronic acid hydrogels, the deprotonation of carboxylic acid moieties at pH > pKa = 3 generates fixed negative charges on the polymer chains, increases hydrophilicity, and electrostatic repulsion, leading to higher water uptake and swelling [N2-F2]. This is a textbook example of pH-induced dissociation-like behavior through ionization, followed by structural expansion.

In contrast, lower pH can cause collapse or reduced swelling. The evidence also notes that hydrogel dissolution can occur in some pH media, which changes the apparent structural behavior [N6-R3]. So pH variation can cause a spectrum of responses: swelling at higher pH, collapse at lower pH, or even partial or total hydrogel dissolution, depending on the polymer chemistry and the surrounding environment [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R3].

#### Ionizable groups vs. crosslinking chemistry
Ionizable groups are the primary sensors in pH-responsive hydrogels. The review explains that these groups can achieve targeted and regulated drug release by exhibiting conformational or solubility changes [N1-R2][N1-F1]. For example, the pKa of poly(acrylic acid) is around 4.5–5.0, and at pH > 5, acidic moieties become ionized, developing a negative charge on the polymer chains [N3-R1]. Similarly, hyaluronic acid hydrogels show pH-dependent swelling because HA’s deprotonation at pH > pKa = 3 generates fixed negative charges and electrostatic repulsion, increasing swelling [N2-F2]. This shows that the pH response is driven by the **ionizable functionality** of the polymer.

Crosslinking chemistry also matters because it determines how the hydrogel holds together and how sensitive that structure is to pH. The evidence explains that hydrogels can be chemically crosslinked by covalent bonds or physically crosslinked by secondary interactions such as hydrogen bonding [N3-F3]. Chemical crosslinking provides structural stability, while physical crosslinking may allow more reversible or sensitive pH responses. The evidence indicates that the **most sensitive mechanisms** are those tied to **swelling**, **diffusion**, and any **matrix relaxation** mechanism. In practical terms, pH variation most directly affects release when it changes the hydrogel’s **porosity, surface area, and effective diffusion path**. When the hydrogel swells, it opens up pathways for drug diffusion; when it collapses, it narrows or blocks those pathways. The review emphasizes that varying the matrix material and environmental conditions leads to different release kinetics, so pH can act as a tuning parameter rather than a fixed trigger [N2-F2]. In short, the mechanisms most sensitive to pH variation are **swelling-driven release**, **ionization-induced conformational changes**, and any **diffusion or transport mechanism** that depends on the hydrogel’s physical state [N1-F1][N2-F2][N1-R4].

The evidence base supports a clear pattern: pH variation can produce **faster, slower, or biphasic release** depending on the hydrogel chemistry and the pH environment.

#### Examples of faster, slower, or biphasic release at different pH values
One of the clearest examples is the **hyaluronic acid hydrogel study**, which reports pH-dependent swelling and links that swelling to release behavior [N2-F2]. This is a strong example of faster release at higher pH, showing that the hydrogel becomes more permeable or swollen under physiological conditions. The evidence shows that pH can shift the kinetics from **diffusion-controlled** to **Case II transport-controlled** or **hybrid behavior**. Dissolution and solubility effects are important because they can modulate pH-dependent release by altering the effective diffusivity of the drug, the hydrogel’s porosity, and the apparent release mechanism. ### 5) Bottom line: how pH variation affects the overall system

Taken together, the evidence supports a consistent picture. pH variation affects hydrogel-based delivery systems through three intertwined mechanisms:
